# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
- **YAML syntax errors remain silent at RUNTIME** (an unparseable file falls
  back to defaults) — `check` is the only place they ar…

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
- **YAML syntax errors remain silent at RUNTIME** (an unparseable file falls
  back to defaults) — `check` is the only place they ar…

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
- **YAML syntax errors remain silent at RUNTIME** (an unparseable file falls

Good — `_resolveSessionNameMatch` returns the fallback pick (`pool.first`) even when ambiguous (only calls `onAmbiguous` then still returns the newest). So `metadata` is non-null in the ambiguous case too. The fix covers:
- exact id resume → metadata.id
- name resume → resolved match id (incl. ambiguity fallback)
- No name → no resume target; new session created after sweep (no race — the new session's file is created after the sweep finishes since it's awaited).

One question: in the ambiguous case, the user might pick a DIFFERENT session from the picker (`_offerStartupSessionChoice`) after boot. Could the sweep have deleted that alternative pick? The sweep ran before the picker is offered, so a same-named session that the user might choose could be deleted by the sweep if it's old, unnamed... wait, no — same-named means it has a name, and `keepNamed: true` default protects named sessions. With `keepNamed: false`, a same-named alternative session could be deleted while the user is looking at the picker. That's a very narrow edge (requires `keepNamed: false` + ambiguous names + over cap + user picks an old one). With `keepNamed: false`, the user has explicitly said named sessions are not protected, so it's arguably intended behavior. Not blocking; maybe worth a suggestion note. Actually — the first review round already covered "resume with keepNamed: false is unprotected" and the fix exempted only the resolved id. The ambiguous-picker alternative remains theoretically vulnerable under keepNamed:false, but that's the documented semantics of keepNamed:false. I'll consider a suggestion.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
- **YAML syntax errors remain silent at RUNTIME** (an unparseable file falls
  back to defaults) — `check` is the only place they ar…

name: self-settings

  Configure fa (flutter_agent_harness) itself by editing the exact config

  ohmypi").
when_to_use: Reconfiguring fa itself — settings, provider, models, memory,
  tools, cubes, MCP, redaction, skills access, themes/TUI appearance — on
  any host (CLI headless, REPL, app), by editing the YAML config the CLI
  persists (themes also via ~/.fah/themes/*.json), never by guessing keys.
argument-hint: "[what to configure, e.g. 'point project memory at ./memory']"

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.

5. Boot: `_retentionBootCheck` runs even when `sweep: off` and cap configured — walks usage to emit the note. That's fine (section touched).

6. Performance: `_retentionBootCheck` awaits the full usage walk before session open. For a huge sessions root this adds boot latency, but only when the section is configured (opt-in). Acceptable, documented.

7. `_initializeSession` — the name-resolution now happens BEFORE `_sweepHeaderOnlySessions()` too. Note ordering: name resolution opens repo.list() — the header-only sweep previously ran first. Does moving the sweep after name-resolution change the gh-1660 header-only sweep semantics? The header-only sweep trashes one-line files older than 10 min. `_sessionNameMatches` runs `repo.list()` — would it now list header-only files that would have been swept? `repo.list()` presumably reads metadata from the header line; header-only files are still valid sessions with metadata (they're only "empty" of records). Before this PR: sweep ran first (fire-and-forget, unawaited), so races existed anyway. The ordering change is benign: the sweep is unawaited in both versions. Not an issue.

8. The `metadata != null` resume path — `_loadSession(metadata)` — if the sweep had (erroneously) deleted it, load fails. With the fix the target is exempt. The race remains only for OTHER sessions becoming live mid-sweep — handled by E2 re-check.

9. `_liveIds` in boot — `config.presenceStore` — set? In AgentCliConfig, `presenceStore` is injectable; bin wires FileSessionPresenceStore. In the boot test they pass `presence`. If null (some embeders), `_liveIds` returns `const {}` — meaning "no live info" → treats all as non-live. Hmm — presenceStore null DISABLES the live exemption rather than failing closed. The doc comment says "null disables the live exemption (tests without presence)". Is there a production path where the boot check runs with presenceStore null? bin wires it always; AgentCliConfig default null only in tests/embeders that don't wire it. The app (flutter) doesn't boot the CLI. Acceptable — though a fail-closed purist would prefer aborting the sweep when presenceStore is null in a real boot. But the sweep only runs when the user opts in; a host without presence wiring would then delete non-live sessions believing them not live. Embeders other than the CLI bin could hit this (e.g., a future daemon). It's a design seam choice, documented in the constructor doc. I'd rate it a SUGESTION at most. Actually — fail-closed posture is a key PR claim ("fail-closed: a presence probe failure aborts the sweep"). A null store isn't a "failure" but an absent probe; the sweep proceeds without live protection. For the CLI (the only boot surface wired today) the store is always present. I'll note as SUGESTION.

10. `bin/fah_runapp.dart` — `readRetention()` is defined but for the `list` verb it's called even without a cap — `loadCliConfig` re-reads the config file. Trivial.

11. In `session_clean_command.dart`: `on Object catch (error)` prints `session clean failed: $error` and returns 1 — the error message may contain a stack-less description. Fine.

12. `formatRetentionBytes`: `value == value.roundToDouble()` for value like 1.048576 (1024*1024 exactly → 1.0 → "1 MB"); for 150 → 1.46 → "1.5 KB". OK. For value ≥ 100 e.g. 150 → "150". OK.

14. Duplicate walk: `/sessions` footer walk runs `usage()` again even though `fa session list` could... fine, one-shot CLI.

16. Potential missed deletion: `cleanupEmptySessions` interplay — not in scope.

17. CHANGELOG entry — accurate.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
- **YAML syntax errors remain silent at RUNTIME** (an unparseable file falls
  back to defaults) — `check` is the only place they ar…

Let me do a couple more exhaustive checks on things nobody flagged yet:

1. `_headerFacts` reads `maxLines: 1` — reads only first line. The header must be line 1. OK, consistent with repo convention (`session` header record first line).

2. `SessionRetentionConfig.fromYaml` — `maxTotalBytes` int parse: yaml `5368709120` parses as int on VM (64-bit) — fine. `value is num` → round. A string "5GB" → note + default. OK.

3. `usage()` — top-level `--slug--` dirs scanned; sessions directly under root? The repo layout: `<root>/<encoded-cwd>/<timestamp>_<id>.jsonl`. Wait — actually from `_scanSlugDir`, transcripts live in slug dirs. Fine.

4. `enforceAtBoot` when `sweep: off` and over cap: `overCapSweepOff` note rendered by `sessionSweepReportLines` → printed at boot. Good (E5).

5. Boot: `_retentionBootCheck` runs even when `sweep: off` and cap configured — walks usage to emit the note. That's fine (section touched).

6. Performance: `_retentionBootCheck` awaits the full usage walk before session open. For a huge sessions root this adds boot latency, but only when the section is configured (opt-in). Acceptable, documented.

7. `_initializeSession` — the name-resolution now happens BEFORE `_sweepHeaderOnlySessions()` too. Note ordering: name resolution opens repo.list() — the header-only sweep previously ran first. Does moving the sweep after name-resolution change the gh-1660 header-only sweep semantics? The header-only sweep trashes one-line files older than 10 min. `_sessionNameMatches` runs `repo.list()` — would it now list header-only files that would have been swept? `repo.list()` presumably reads metadata from the header line; header-only files are still valid sessions with metadata (they're only "empty" of records). Before this PR: sweep ran first (fire-and-forget, unawaited), so races existed anyway. The ordering change is benign: the sweep is unawaited in both versions. Not an issue.

8. The `metadata != null` resume path — `_loadSession(metadata)` — if the sweep had (erroneously) deleted it, load fails. With the fix the target is exempt. The race remains only for OTHER sessions becoming live mid-sweep — handled by E2 re-check.

9. `_liveIds` in boot — `config.presenceStore` — set? In AgentCliConfig, `presenceStore` is injectable; bin wires FileSessionPresenceStore. In the boot test they pass `presence`. If null (some embeders), `_liveIds` returns `const {}` — meaning "no live info" → treats all as non-live. Hmm — presenceStore null DISABLES the live exemption rather than failing closed. The doc comment says "null disables the live exemption (tests without presence)". Is there a production path where the boot check runs with presenceStore null? bin wires it always; AgentCliConfig default null only in tests/embeders that don't wire it. The app (flutter) doesn't boot the CLI. Acceptable — though a fail-closed purist would prefer aborting the sweep when presenceStore is null in a real boot. But the sweep only runs when the user opts in; a host without presence wiring would then delete non-live sessions believing them not live. Embeders other than the CLI bin could hit this (e.g., a future daemon). It's a design seam choice, documented in the constructor doc. I'd rate it a SUGESTION at most. Actually — fail-closed posture is a key PR claim ("fail-closed: a presence probe failure aborts the sweep"). A null store isn't a "failure" but an absent probe; the sweep proceeds without live protection. For the CLI (the only boot surface wired today) the store is always present. I'll note as SUGESTION.

10. `bin/fah_runapp.dart` — `readRetention()` is defined but for the `list` verb it's called even without a cap — `loadCliConfig` re-reads the config file. Trivial.

11. In `session_clean_command.dart`: `on Object catch (error)` prints `session clean failed: $error` and returns 1 — the error message may contain a stack-less description. Fine.

12. `formatRetentionBytes`: `value == value.roundToDouble()` for value like 1.048576 (1024*1024 exactly → 1.0 → "1 MB"); for 150 → 1.46 → "1.5 KB". OK. For value ≥ 100 e.g. 150 → "150". OK.

13. `sessionUsageFooterLine` — computes usage; for the `/sessions` in-REPL path it constructs a NEW sweper without presence — fine, usage-only walk doesn't need presence.

14. Duplicate walk: `/sessions` footer walk runs `usage()` again even though `fa session list` could... fine, one-shot CLI.

15. Check the `.tools` sweep: `_fs.remove('$dir/.tools/${session.sessionId}.yaml')` — dir is the slug dir. Consistent with scan (`'${slugDir.path}/.tools/$sessionId.yaml'`). Good.

16. Potential missed deletion: `cleanupEmptySessions` interplay — not in scope.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
- **YAML syntax errors remain silent at RUNTIME** (an unparseable file falls

🚨 Formatting drift — `dart format` is not clean on 4 touched files

`dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed` (Dart 3.13.5) reports changes in:

- `lib/src/cli/cli_config.dart` (2 missing blank lines, e.g. after the `sessions` getter at line 936)

- `test/session_retention_config_test.dart`
- `test/cli/session_clean_cli_test.dart`

`origin/main`'s version of `cli_config.dart` is format-clean under the same SDK, so this PR introduced the drift. The pre-commit hook self-heals staged files and CI does not gate on format, so nothing breaks — but the next commit from any author with the hook will reformat these lines, adding noise to a future diff.

Suggested: run `dart format lib/src/cli/cli_config.dart lib/src/config/config_service.dart test/session_retention_config_test.dart test/cli/session_clean_cli_test.dart` before merge.

💡 `presenceStore: null` silently disables the live exemption instead of failing closed

`_liveIds()` maps a null store to an empty live-set (treated as "nothing is live"), while a *failing* probe aborts the sweep. The doc comment scopes null to tests, and today every production boot path wires a real store (`bin/fah_runapp.dart` for the CLI; the clean verb passes one too) — so this is hardening, not a bug.

But the PR's stated posture is fail-closed ("a presence probe failure aborts the sweep instead of risking a live session"). A future embedder host that runs `enforceAtBoot()` without wiring a presence store would sweep live sessions while believing none are live.

Suggested: in `enforceAtBoot()`, treat `presenceStore == null` the same as a failed probe (abort with a note), or add an explicit `allowMissingPresence` flag so the test convenience is opt-in rather than the default shape.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
